content: It includes citations of scientific articles, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and operational manuals, as well as acknowledgments of contributors to guidelines and research efforts. 1. In 2003, a study was conducted to evaluate treatment strategies for Schistosoma mansoni in a highly endemic area near Lake Albert, Uganda. The findings were published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 2. Raso et al. (2004) investigated the efficacy and side effects of praziquantel in treating Schistosoma mansoni infections within a community in western Côte d’Ivoire. Their results were published in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 3. Sousa-Figueiredo et al. (2012) assessed the performance and safety of praziquantel for treating intestinal schistosomiasis in infants and preschool-aged children. The study was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 4. Stelma et al. (1995) examined the efficacy and side effects of praziquantel in an epidemic focus of Schistosoma mansoni. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 5. Zwang and Olliaro (2014) conducted a meta-analysis to evaluate the clinical efficacy and tolerability of praziquantel for intestinal and urinary schistosomiasis. The study was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 6. Kernell et al. (2018) explored the risks of adverse swallowing events and choking during deworming treatments for preschool-aged children. Their findings were published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 7. Fleming et al. (2009) conducted a process evaluation of Uganda’s national schistosomiasis control program from 2003 to 2006, focusing on perceptions, attitudes, and constraints. The study was published in Parasitology. 8. Nwaorgu et al. (2005) evaluated the acceptability of a school-based schistosomiasis and intestinal helminthiasis control program in Nigeria. Their findings were published in Tropical Medicine and International Health. 9. A 2015 study in The Lancet Global Health compared the cost-effectiveness of community-wide, integrated mass drug administration strategies for schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminthiasis. 10. Leslie et al. (2011) analyzed the cost-effectiveness of school-based and community-distributed mass drug administration programs for controlling schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminths in Niger. The study was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 11. Burnim et al. (2017) conducted a systematic review of community-based, school-based, and combined delivery modes for mass drug administration programs targeting school-aged children with schistosomiasis. The findings were published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 12. Cabello et al. (2016) investigated Schistosoma mansoni infection rates and related knowledge among schoolchildren in an endemic area of Minas Gerais, Brazil, prior to implementing educational interventions. The study was published in Parasitology. 13. Liu et al. (2014) examined knowledge, attitudes, and practices related to schistosomiasis in two subtypes of a mountainous region in China. The study was published in Infectious Diseases of Poverty. 14. Sacolo et al. (2018) conducted a systematic review of knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding schistosomiasis in sub-Saharan Africa. The findings were published in BMC Infectious Diseases. 15. A 2015 study in Parasites & Vectors explored knowledge, attitudes, and practices toward schistosomiasis among rural populations in Yemen. 16. Muhumuza et al. (2015) investigated the low uptake of mass treatment for intestinal schistosomiasis among schoolchildren in Jinja District, Uganda. The study was published in the Journal of Biosocial Science. 17. Tuhebwe et al. (2015) evaluated the uptake of mass drug administration programs for schistosomiasis control in Koome Islands, Uganda. The findings were published in PLoS One. 18. Krentel et al. (2017) reviewed factors influencing the motivation of community drug distributors in controlling and eliminating neglected tropical diseases. The study was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 19. Macfarlane et al. (2014) conducted a systematic review and policy analysis on the role of community drug distributors in mass drug administration programs for neglected tropical diseases. The study was published in the Journal of Global Health. 20. Fleming et al. (2016) used a mixed-methods approach to evaluate the performance of community drug distributors in controlling neglected tropical diseases. The study was published in Parasites & Vectors. 21. Taylor-Robinson et al. (2015) reviewed the effects of deworming drugs on nutritional indicators, hemoglobin levels, and school performance in children. The findings were published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 22. Zwang and Olliaro (2017) conducted a meta-analysis on the efficacy and safety of praziquantel at 40 mg/kg in preschool-aged and school-aged children. The study was published in Parasites & Vectors. 23. Danso-Appiah et al. (2013) reviewed drugs for treating Schistosoma mansoni infections. The findings were published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 24. Kramer et al. (2014) reviewed drugs for treating urinary schistosomiasis. The study was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 25. Ndibazza et al. (2010) investigated the effects of deworming during pregnancy on maternal and perinatal outcomes in Uganda. The study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 26. Freeman et al. (2017) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the impact of sanitation on infectious diseases and nutritional status. The study was published in the International Journal of Hygiene and Environmental Health. 27. Sclar et al. (2018) explored the relationship between sanitation and mental and social well-being through a systematic review and qualitative synthesis. The study was published in Social Science & Medicine. 28. WHO guidelines for drinking-water quality, safe recreational water environments, and sanitation and health were accessed and reviewed for their relevance to schistosomiasis control. 29. Braun et al. (2018) reviewed the effectiveness of water treatment processes against schistosome cercariae. The study was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 30. Grimes et al. (2015) reviewed the roles of water, sanitation, and hygiene in reducing schistosomiasis. The study was published in Parasites & Vectors. 31. Dawson (2003) reviewed the environmental fate and effects of the molluscicide Bayluscide. The study was published in the Journal of Great Lakes Research. 32. Andrews et al. (1983) examined the biology and toxicology of molluscicides, including Bayluscide. The study was published in Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 33. Takougang et al. (2007) evaluated community acceptance of low-dose niclosamide as a molluscicide for schistosomiasis control in Cameroon. The study was published in the Annals of Tropical Medicine and Parasitology. 34. Knopp et al. (2012) studied the implementation of urogenital schistosomiasis elimination in Zanzibar using an integrated multidisciplinary approach. The findings were published in Parasites & Vectors. 35. Lo et al. (2018) assessed the impact and cost-effectiveness of snail control in achieving schistosomiasis control targets. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA. 36. WHO operational manuals and guidelines for molluscicide use, laboratory testing, and risk assessment were reviewed for their application in schistosomiasis control programs. 37. Barenbold et al. (2018) translated prevalence thresholds for Schistosoma mansoni from the Kato-Katz technique into point-of-care diagnostic tests. The study was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 38. Sato et al. (2018) evaluated the usefulness of environmental DNA for detecting Schistosoma mansoni occurrence sites in Madagascar. The study was published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases. 39. A 2019 study in PLoS One explored the detection of Schistosoma japonicum and Oncomelania hupensis quadrasi environmental DNA for schistosomiasis surveillance in the Philippines. 40. Contributors to the WHO guidelines included experts from various institutions worldwide, such as the University of Georgia, the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, and the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute.
